title: Middle East NOC oil and gas strategies beyond the crisis | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Q&A with Neivan Boroujerdi (by Simon Flowers) finds the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz closure split Gulf NOCs: Aramco and ADNOC earned US$35bn extra OCF via bypass pipelines while QatarEnergy lost 17% of liquefaction capacity and US$10bn OCF. The crisis is accelerating bypass-pipeline build-outs and overseas gas/LNG diversification (XRG, Aramco, QE, KUFPEC), while IOCs remain keen on long-life, low-cost Gulf resources.

themes.theme: War impact: Hormuz closure splits Gulf NOC winners and losers

insights.claim: Gulf-based NOCs all lost production over nine months of the Iran war because the Strait of Hormuz closure and infrastructure damage constrained exports.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Hormuz closure is a physical supply shock hitting every Gulf exporter, not just price volatility.
insights.locator: How has the war affected Middle East NOCs’ performance?

insights.claim: Alternative oil export routes bypassing Hormuz acted as an insurance policy, letting Saudi Aramco and ADNOC generate US$35 billion more operating cash flow in 2026 than Wood Mackenzie forecast at the start of the year.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Bypass infrastructure turned a crisis into a cash windfall for Aramco and ADNOC via high prices.
insights.quote: Saudi Aramco and ADNOC have generated US$35 billion more operating cash flow (OCF) in 2026 than we forecast at the start of the year.
insights.locator: All Gulf-based NOCs took a production hit

insights.claim: Northern Gulf producers Kuwait and Iraq had no bypass export option, and there is no alternative shipping route at all for LNG out of the Gulf.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Kuwaiti/Iraqi volumes and Gulf LNG are the most exposed to Hormuz disruption.
insights.locator: That option was not available to producers

insights.claim: QatarEnergy, the world's biggest LNG producer, lost 17% of its liquefaction capacity to war damage and has exported only minimal cargoes since the Strait effectively closed in February, leaving its operating cash flow US$10 billion below Wood Mackenzie's start-of-year forecast.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A major chunk of global LNG supply is impaired, supporting LNG prices and non-Gulf suppliers.
insights.quote: lost 17% of its liquefaction capacity to war damage
insights.locator: That option was not available to producers

insights.claim: QatarEnergy's cash shortfall occurred despite the start-up of its new 18-mmtpa Golden Pass liquefaction facility on the US Gulf Coast.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: US-based capacity only partly offsets lost Gulf output for Qatar.
insights.locator: That option was not available to producers

themes.theme: Resilience: bypass pipelines and the geography constraint

insights.claim: After the crisis, building resilience and securing alternative export routes has become a top priority for export-dependent Gulf economies.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Expect capex redirected to pipelines and bypass export infrastructure.
insights.quote: access to alternative export routes now a must for these export-dependent economies
insights.locator: What lessons have we learned from the crisis?

insights.claim: The UAE is adding 1.5 million b/d of capacity to its 1.8 million b/d pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: UAE bypass capacity rising to ~3.3 million b/d strengthens its export reliability premium.
insights.locator: Building resilience into the system

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's alternative export pipeline capacity could rise from 7 million b/d to up to 10 million b/d by 2030, technically enough to carry all of its exports without Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Saudi supply could become largely Hormuz-proof by 2030, reducing the risk premium on its barrels.
insights.quote: could rise from 7 million b/d to up to 10 million b/d by 2030
insights.locator: Building resilience into the system

insights.claim: Qatar, Kuwait and Iraq face stiffer challenges developing alternative liquids export capacity at scale, and alternative routes for Qatari LNG would realistically require cross-border gas pipeline and liquefaction arrangements that mean ceding sovereign control at significant risk and cost.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Qatar's LNG remains structurally Hormuz-exposed; diversification must come from overseas assets.
insights.quote: Ceding sovereign control of critical parts of the value chain will come with significant risks and costs.
insights.locator: Geography, though, is (almost) everything.

themes.theme: Overseas diversification led by gas and LNG

insights.claim: The war has strengthened Middle East NOCs' long-standing rationale for diversifying overseas, with gas and LNG at the forefront, using government-to-government relationships and existing domestic IOC partnerships (notably in the UAE and Qatar) as routes to deals.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Gulf NOC capital will be a growing bidder for global gas/LNG assets, supporting valuations.
insights.locator: Will Middle East NOCs look to diversify overseas?

insights.claim: ADNOC's international vehicle XRG, launched in December 2024, has built positions in the Americas, Africa and the Caspian and is reportedly targeting a US$15 billion-plus US shale gas position and exploring a stake in LNG Canada.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: XRG is a likely acquirer in US gas and Canadian LNG—relevant for potential targets.
insights.locator: ADNOC: the strategy for XRG

insights.claim: XRG's acquisition of Shell's North West Shelf LNG stake brings its LNG portfolio to 22 mmtpa; reaching its 47 mmtpa goal by 2035 would make ADNOC the fifth-largest LNG supplier globally, with further upstream and downstream integration deals likely.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: ADNOC aims to more than double LNG portfolio in a decade—sustained M&A appetite.
insights.quote: If the ambitious goal of 47 mmtpa by 2035 is achieved, ADNOC would become the fifth-largest LNG supplier globally.
insights.locator: ADNOC: the strategy for XRG

insights.claim: Saudi Aramco is targeting 10 to 20 mmtpa of international LNG supply by 2030, independently and via its reduced stake in MidOcean Energy, and has signed LNG SPAs with US projects Rio Grande and Commonwealth LNG.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Aramco is a growing offtaker/backer for US LNG developers.
insights.locator: Saudi Aramco: Aramco has been pursuing

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates Aramco could have 6 bcfd of surplus domestic gas early next decade, enough for up to 40 mmtpa of LNG exports, making domestic LNG potentially its biggest opportunity.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A possible new Saudi LNG export source would add major supply to the 2030s market.
insights.quote: the biggest opportunity in LNG might be domestic
insights.locator: However, the biggest opportunity in LNG

insights.claim: Foreign participation in Saudi oil and gas production is currently not permitted, but domestic funding needs and gas ambitions may open parts of the Saudi upstream to strategic partners.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A potential opening of Saudi upstream would be a landmark access opportunity for IOCs.
insights.locator: However, the biggest opportunity in LNG

insights.claim: QatarEnergy signed for 7 mmtpa of US LNG via deals with Cheniere and Woodside Energy, which combined with its 70% Golden Pass stake makes it the largest offtaker of US LNG, and more such deals are likely.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Qatar is hedging Hormuz risk by sourcing US LNG—supportive for US LNG contracting.
insights.quote: undoubtedly a response to events in the Gulf
insights.locator: QatarEnergy: QE recently signed up

insights.claim: QatarEnergy has used relationships with domestic partners to build an exploration-led international upstream portfolio that could produce over 200,000 boed next decade, with organic investment and possibly M&A expected.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: QE may emerge as an upstream acquirer beyond LNG.
insights.locator: QE has also leveraged its relationships

insights.claim: Kuwait's KUFPEC produces around 80,000 boed internationally and, despite entering offshore Brazil and progressing Malaysia's Lang Lebah gas project, needs more business development to reach its 200,000 boed target.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: KUFPEC must more than double output—likely buyer of international upstream assets.
insights.locator: KUFPEC: Kuwait Petroleum’s international business

themes.theme: IOC appetite for Middle East resources

insights.claim: IOC appetite for Middle East investment remains intact, evidenced by ExxonMobil, BP and ConocoPhillips deals in Iraq and BP and TotalEnergies' Bab Gas Cap deal in the UAE.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: War has not deterred majors from Gulf resource access.
insights.locator: Do IOCs still want to invest in the Middle East?

insights.claim: Kuwait's extension of enhanced technical service agreements to BP and Shell may be a precursor to offshore investment opportunities for IOCs in Kuwait.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Possible new offshore access in Kuwait for majors.
insights.locator: Do IOCs still want to invest in the Middle East?

insights.claim: Big Oil faces declining production over the next decade, and discovered long-life, low-cost Middle East resources can address part of that longevity gap even though returns are typically modest.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Reserve-life pressure will push majors into lower-return but durable Gulf assets.
insights.quote: Big Oil faces a longevity challenge, with declining production over the next decade.
insights.locator: Big Oil faces a longevity challenge

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects Middle East governments to become increasingly keen to attract foreign investment amid a competitive environment for capital, which could improve terms for IOCs.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Host-country terms may improve for investors.
insights.quote: we expect Middle East governments will be increasingly keen to attract investment in a competitive environment for capital
insights.locator: Big Oil faces a longevity challenge
